This isn't, as many people have posted, a result of "lazy producers", it's a result of cheap owners. Especially in smaller markets, a single producer will write between 2 and 4 30 minutes shows EVERY SINGLE DAY.. It used to be that a producer would write part of one show, and reporters would write their own stories. That's not the case anymore, especially as smaller market tv newsrooms cut budgets. I worked at a smaller market tv station about 10 years ago and watched as they got sold from Gannett to Sinclair. Our newsroom added 2 newscasts and had our budget literally cut in half. What used to be carefully crafted news turned into a race to get enough content to fill a half hour. For example, one producer would come in at 2, have 3 hours to get enough content for the 5, then after the 5 have to get enough to fill the 9. On weekends it was worse. We would literally have 1 reporter and photographer during the day, then at night we would have 1 photog and the anchor. The anchor would write the 6, 9, and 10 (we didn't have a 5 on weekends), and the night photog doubled as an editor for those 3 newscasts. That's not enough time to do any "real" news. You have whatever your lead story is, a few basic stories, and then it's trying to fill time until the newscast is over.

TL;DR: This is what happens when you have newsrooms run for profit and not for public good.

Do you still live with your parents? If you do, try to be more aggressive with your role in feeding the cat. Insist that you handle all his food, and talk with his vet to get him on a weightloss food, and know exactly how much of it to feed. Weightloss food will generally be pricier than the regular stuff, but it's important to buy him a food geared for weightloss. Firstly, because they usually have more fibre, which will keep him feeling full for longer, and secondly (most importantly) because the nutrient ratios will be different than that of a regular maintenance diet. Put simply, if you try to get your cat to lose weight by feeding him only a portion of his regular food, then he is only getting a portion of the essential vitamins he needs. If you feed him say 80% of his calories with a maintenance diet, then he is only getting 80% the vitamin A, E, taurine, etc. that he needs. Weight loss diets are designed to be lower calories, but have 100% of the vitamins kitty needs.

Also, you can tell your dad that cats are more likely to get hyperthyroidism instead of hypothyroidism. This means their metabolisms are more likely to be too fast, and they will burn too many calories, and be too skinny. Hypothyroidism on the other hand is so extremely rare in cats I've never seen it in-clinic. Not to say that it can't happen, but the odds are that your cat is not hypothyroid. Your vet can check his thyroid level through a simple blood test.
